title: The Crayon Box That Talked
author: Shane DeRolf

demand_candidate.rationale: Concrete colours and classroom objects combine with belonging and cooperation themes, producing strong matching, sorting, AAC, and September community activities.

book_summary: A girl in a toy store overhears a box of crayons arguing — Yellow and Green dislike Red, and no one likes Orange. She buys the box, takes it home, and uses every crayon to draw a picture, and as the crayons watch her combine all the colors together they realize each of them was needed to make the picture complete.

fringe_justifications.red: Red is the crayon disliked by Yellow and Green at the start of the story: <cite index="2-1">Yellow hates Red, so does Green, and no one likes Orange!</cite>
fringe_justifications.orange: Orange is singled out as the crayon disliked by everyone in the box: <cite index="2-1">Yellow hates Red, so does Green, and no one likes Orange!</cite>
fringe_justifications.yellow: Yellow is named as the crayon who starts the conflict by hating Red: <cite index="2-1">Yellow hates Red, so does Green, and no one likes Orange!</cite>
fringe_justifications.green: Green joins Yellow in disliking Red at the outset of the story: <cite index="2-1">Yellow hates Red, so does Green, and no one likes Orange!</cite>
fringe_justifications.blue: Blue is one of the crayons the girl uses as she colors her picture: <cite index="17-2,17-3">They watched me as I coloured · with Red and Blue and Green. And Black and White and Orange, and every colour in between.</cite>
fringe_justifications.purple: The purple crayon is shown with a distinct angry expression, covering his ears and frowning, used to discuss feelings during the story.
fringe_justifications.girl: A girl overhears the crayons arguing in the toy store and is the one who buys the box and resolves the conflict: <cite index="4-5">In The Crayon Box that Talked, a girl goes in a toy store and is drawn to a crayon box that doesn't get along.</cite>
fringe_justifications.toy store: The story opens with the crayons bickering while sitting on a shelf in a toy store, before the girl overhears and buys them: <cite index="12-1">The various colors lodged on the toy-store shelf express their dislike for one another and lament that "Something here is wrong!"</cite>
fringe_justifications.draw: The girl lays out the crayons and draws a full scene using every color, which is the turning point of the story: <cite index="3-6">She lays out her new drawing tools and creates a scene using all the colors, until the crayons realize, "when we get together.../ The picture is complete."</cite>
fringe_justifications.picture: The finished picture, made from all the colors together, is what convinces the crayons to get along: <cite index="13-15">But when we get together…The picture is complete.</cite>
fringe_justifications.together: The crayons' realization that being together makes the picture whole is the book's central message: <cite index="13-14,13-15">We are a box of crayons, each one of us unique. But when we get together…The picture is complete.</cite>

grounding_note: Confirmed via multiple sources (Publishers Weekly, Penguin Random House, Prindle Institute, Goodreads reviews, and a full poem-text PDF) that this is the 1997 Shane DeRolf/Michael Letzig picture book about a box of anthropomorphic crayons (Yellow, Green, Red, Orange, Blue, Black, White, etc.) who argue in a toy store until a girl buys them and draws a picture using all the colors together, teaching a lesson about diversity and unity. Exact page-by-page sequence of every crayon's dialogue was not fully retrieved, but the core plot, characters, and ending message are consistently corroborated across sources.
